title: 3 ספרים שכיף לקרוא שוב ולנחש מה יקרה

stage.need: Retelling a familiar story in order and guessing what comes next. CDC lists 'Tells what comes next in a well-known story' at 4 years and answering simple questions about a book at 5.
stage.age_caveat: Milestones are what most children do by an age, not a deadline. The slides say בסביבות and יש שמגיעים לזה קודם ויש שאחר כך.

dev_sources.title: Milestones by 4 Years
dev_sources.publisher: CDC, Learn the Signs. Act Early.
dev_sources.quote: Tells what comes next in a well-known story / Read with your child. Ask him what's happening in the story and what he thinks might happen next. / Use words, such as "first," "second," and "finally." When playing, telling stories, or doing chores, ask your child what comes next. This will help your child learn about the order of events. / Continue to teach your child skills to play with others, such as using words, sharing toys, and taking turns. / Teach your child to stop and wait when excited by playing red light, green light, or freeze dance (play music, turn it off, and have everyone freeze when it stops).
dev_sources.supports: Books: 'Tells what comes next in a well-known story' is a cognitive milestone by 4 years, which maps exactly to the repetition/predict angle (the story has to be well-known, i.e. familiar). CDC recommends asking what might happen next while reading, and asking 'what comes next' when telling stories to help children learn the order of events. Games: CDC recommends teaching turn-taking as a play skill at 4, and practising stopping and waiting through games. Caveat: the stop-and-wait tip names movement games (red light green light, freeze dance), not board games; the 4-year page suggests 'simple games, such as Tic-Tac-Toe or matching games', and the rule-following milestone itself appears only on the 5-year page.

dev_sources.title: Milestones by 5 Years
dev_sources.publisher: CDC, Learn the Signs. Act Early.
dev_sources.quote: Follows rules or takes turns when playing games with other children / Teach your child to follow rules in games. For example, play simple board games, card games, or Simon Says. / Answers simple questions about a book or story after you read or tell it to him / Tells a story she heard or made up with at least two events. For example, a cat was stuck in a tree and a firefighter saved it / Read to your child. Ask questions, such as "What is happening in the picture?" and "What do you think will happen next?" / Encourage your child to "read" by looking at the pictures and telling the story.
dev_sources.supports: Games: following rules or taking turns in games with other children is a listed social/emotional milestone by 5 years, and CDC explicitly suggests simple board and card games as a way to teach rule-following. Books: answering questions about a book after reading and telling a story with at least two events are listed language milestones by 5; CDC's own tip is to ask 'What do you think will happen next?' while reading and to let the child 'read' by telling the story from the pictures. Caveat: CDC defines milestones as things most children (75% or more) can do by that age, so this is a typical range, not a target every child hits. Six quotes kept so you can pick; the first two are games, the rest books.

dev_sources.title: Tips to Help Your Child Enjoy Reading Aloud
dev_sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics, Committee on Early Childhood)
dev_sources.quote: Let your child choose the book even if it means reading the same book over and over. / Invite your child to "read" to you from a familiar book that he has memorized from having heard it so often read to him. / Stop and ask about the illustrations or what your child thinks will happen next. The answers may amaze you.
dev_sources.supports: AAP parent tips that endorse re-reading the same book, letting the child 'read' (retell) a familiar book back, and stopping to ask what will happen next. Covers repetition, retelling and prediction in one page. Caveat: filed under the grade-school section, though the tips are not age-limited; it is practical advice, not a research claim.

dev_sources.title: How to Share Books with Your Preschooler
dev_sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics, Committee on Early Childhood)
dev_sources.quote: Sharing books with your children can help them learn to talk better and get them ready to listen and learn in school. / Tell you the story in a favorite book in their own words. / “Correct” you if you skip a word or page in a favorite book.
dev_sources.supports: Under '4 Year Olds Can:', AAP lists retelling a favourite book in their own words and correcting the parent if a word or page is skipped in a favourite book, which shows the familiarity that repeated reading builds. Under 'What Parents Can Do:' it adds 'Ask your child to tell you about the pictures and the story.' Caveat: older page (2013, content copyright 1994); it lists what 4-year-olds can do, not research findings.

dev_sources.title: Executive Function Activities for 3- to 5-year-olds
dev_sources.publisher: Center on the Developing Child at Harvard University
dev_sources.quote: Their early stories tend to be a series of events, each one related to the one before, but lacking any larger structure. With practice, children develop more complex and organized plots. As the complexity of the storytelling grows, children practice holding and manipulating information in working memory. / Revisiting the story, either by reviewing pictures or words, supports more intentional organization and greater elaboration. / Children have to inhibit the tendency to mark the picture that matches, while also remembering the game’s rule.
dev_sources.supports: Books: storytelling is practice; children's stories start as chains of events and become more organised with practice; revisiting a story through its pictures or words supports more organised, elaborated retelling. Games: simple rule games (bingo/lotto with a twist rule) ask children to hold a rule in mind and inhibit an automatic response. Caveat: the storytelling section is about children telling and revisiting their own stories (written down by an adult), not specifically about reading picture books; the game quote describes a modified 'opposites' bingo, not a standard board game.

dev_sources.title: WWC Intervention Report: Dialogic Reading (revised February 8, 2007)
dev_sources.publisher: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
dev_sources.quote: Dialogic Reading is an interactive shared picture book reading practice designed to enhance young children’s language and literacy skills. / During the shared reading practice, the adult and the child switch roles so that the child learns to become the storyteller with the assistance of the adult who functions as an active listener and questioner. / Dialogic Reading was found to have positive effects on oral language and no discernible effects on phonological processing.
dev_sources.supports: A US government evidence review of five studies (over 300 preschool children) rated dialogic reading, where the child becomes the storyteller and the adult asks questions, as having positive effects on oral language. Caveats: no discernible effect on phonological processing; studies were in English, in centre-based settings, ages 3 to 5 or preschool, mostly economically disadvantaged children; the report is from 2007. Supports 'talking about the book can support language', not literacy broadly.

products.popularity_reasoning: Strong Israel-specific signal: Sifriyat Pijama distribution of 140,800 copies (2022-2023) to young kindergarten classes, plus current availability at both national chains and the publisher. There is no bestseller-list evidence; its reach comes mainly from the programme.
products.developmental_relevance: The child can retell the chain in order ('מי החליף את מי?'), predict the next replacement before the page turn, and match each character to their job and tool (comb, rolling pin, stethoscope). Structure: A rhyming replacement chain. A brother and sister on their way to a flute lesson stand in for a sick flute player in a parade. Then each helper must be replaced in turn ('ומי יחליף את...?'): the barber plays music on a comb, the baker steps in for the barber, the doctor for the baker, and so on, each time with the same rhymed request for help. The question-and-answer pattern repeats on every spread, so the child can guess who will be asked next and what odd job they will do.
products.parent_tip_source: On a second read, pause at every 'ומי יחליף את...?' and let the child guess who comes next, then ask the Sifriyat Pijama recall question 'מי החליף את מי?' and let the child retell the chain. The pause-and-guess part is my suggestion; the recall questions come from the Sifriyat Pijama guide: 'שאלות שחזור והבנת העלילה – מדוע בחרו הילדים לעזור לנגנים? למה הם נאלצו להפסיק? מי החליף את מי? כיצד עזרה כל אחת מהדמויות?'

products.developmental_relevance: The child can retell who asked for porridge in order (Sifriyat Pijama links it to the classic finger rhyme 'סבתא בישלה דייסה': 'למי היא נתנה ולמי לא נשאר?'), predict at each refrain whether any porridge will be left, and act out the two simultaneous storylines. Structure: Two strands told in parallel with a repeated refrain. Hanna-Banana is hurrying down the street to Granny's house (refrain: 'בינתיים חנה-בננה מאוד ממהרת…'), while Granny gives the porridge she cooked for her granddaughter to each neighbour who asks, one after another, until not a drop is left; then Hanna-Banana arrives and comforts Granny. Every page repeats the same beat (someone asks, Granny gives, meanwhile Hanna hurries), so the child can predict that the next visitor will also get porridge and that the pot is emptying.
products.parent_tip_source: At every refrain 'בינתיים חנה-בננה מאוד ממהרת…' stop and ask the child what is happening now, then at the end play the finger rhyme and ask who got porridge and who did not. Source: Sifriyat Pijama parent guide: 'בכל פעם שאתם מגיעים למילים "בינתיים חנה-בננה מאוד ממהרת…" תוכלו לבקש מילדיכם לתאר מה הם רואים בתמונה.' and 'תוכלו לשחק עם ילדיכם את משחק האצבעות "סבתא בישלה דייסה". על פי הסיפור "סבתא של חנה בננה בישלה דייסה", למי היא נתנה ולמי לא נשאר?'

products.popularity_reasoning: Strong Israel-specific signal: selected and distributed by Sifriyat Pijama (2024-2025), plus in print at both national chains in hardcover and board book. The 'רב המכר עטור השבחים' line on the retailer and publisher pages is publisher copy that most likely refers to the book's international sales, so I did not count it as Israeli bestseller evidence. Tzomet shows only 1 reader review, so review volume is not a signal.
products.developmental_relevance: Sequence retelling: which animals came and in what order, what each suggested, what the rabbit did, what Taylor did afterwards. Sifriyat Pijama notes that the pictures sit next to the matching lines so young pre-readers can retell the story on their own. Structure: Taylor's block tower collapses. Animals then arrive one after another, and each offers its own fix (Sifriyat Pijama names the ostrich hiding its head, the elephant remembering, the bear getting angry); none helps and each leaves. Finally the rabbit comes and simply listens, and Taylor rebuilds. The fixed loop (animal arrives, suggests, Taylor refuses, animal leaves) lets the child predict that the next animal will also fail and guess what the rabbit will do differently.
products.parent_tip_source: After the first read, ask the sequence questions from the Sifriyat Pijama guide ('אילו חיות הוא פגש?', 'מה הציעו החיות לטיילור?', 'מה עשה הארנב?'), then let the child retell it from the pictures alone and act out each animal's voice and movement. Source quotes: 'לאחר הקריאה הראשונה כדאי לשאול שאלות ש מסייעות להבנת הרצף הסיפורי' and 'ילדים צעירים שטרם רכשו את מיומנות הקריאה יכולים להיעזר בכך כקביים שבעזרתם ינסו ואף יצליחו לספר את הסיפור באופן עצמאי.'
